buildings.name: St. Mary's Church
buildings.fabricLine: Brick walls from the 1270s, spire from 1789
buildings.today: The oldest church still holding services in Berlin, and the one large building in the medieval centre that came through the war standing. Allied bomber crews used it as a navigation landmark, which is part of why the church survived while every street around it did not.
buildings.tell: Look at the base of the tower. The lower courses are rough field stones, the kind you cannot fake with 1980s panels. Then look up: the pointed spire is neo-Gothic, added by Carl Gotthard Langhans in 1789 and 1790, five hundred years younger than the walls under it.

buildings.name: St. Nicholas' Church
buildings.fabricLine: Medieval walls, 1980s roof and twin spires
buildings.today: Berlin oldest building, kept as a roofless shell for four decades and then rebuilt by East Germany between 1981 and 1987. The walls are genuinely medieval. Everything above them, including the two spires everyone photographs, is East German work.
buildings.tell: Stand at the west end and follow the brickwork upward. There is a clear horizontal line where old, uneven, weathered brick gives way to regular modern courses. That line is where 1945 stopped and 1987 started.

buildings.name: Nikolaiviertel
buildings.today: The quarter that reads as Berlin surviving old town is the newest thing in this whole audit. The GDR rebuilt it for the 750th anniversary of the city in 1987, under the architect Guenter Stahn, using the same standardised concrete panels as the housing blocks nearby, dressed in gables.
buildings.tell: Put your hand on a gable wall. Prefabricated panels give you flat, even surfaces and a repeating joint pattern, and the same house type turns up again two streets along. The medieval street lines are real; almost none of the houses on them are.

buildings.name: Rotes Rathaus
buildings.today: Berlin working city hall, built between 1861 and 1869, gutted in the war and rebuilt to the original plans between 1951 and 1956. The design is genuinely 1860s. Most of the brick holding it up is 1950s.
buildings.tell: The terracotta relief frieze that runs around the building at first-floor height is the giveaway. Where it is sharp and complete it was recut after the war; where it is worn and chipped it is original 1870s work. Both are on the same wall.

buildings.name: Neptune Fountain
buildings.today: Reinhold Begas finished this in 1891 as a gift from the city to Wilhelm II, and it stood on the Schlossplatz in front of the palace. It came down with the palace in 1951, went into storage, and was set down on this spot in 1969. The object is entirely original. The address is not.
buildings.tell: Nothing on the fountain itself will tell you. The tell is the setting: a grand baroque-revival fountain designed as the centrepiece of a palace square, now sitting in an open GDR park with no palace in sight.

buildings.name: TV Tower
buildings.today: Opened on 3 October 1969 and never destroyed, never rebuilt, never disguised. The tallest thing in the picture is also one of the most honest.
buildings.tell: No test needed. This is the control case: a Berlin landmark whose date and fabric are the same number.

buildings.name: World Clock
buildings.today: Erich John design, handed over on 30 September 1969, a fortnight of celebrations before the GDR twentieth anniversary. It has been repaired and repainted, and the city names on the ring have been updated as countries changed, but it is the same object.
buildings.tell: Read the ring of city names. Some of them belong to states that no longer exist in that form, which is how you know you are looking at a 1969 object rather than a modern copy of one.

buildings.name: Humboldt Forum
buildings.today: The palace begun in 1443 and rebuilt into a baroque masterwork by Andreas Schlueter between 1698 and 1713 burnt in 1945 and was blown up by the GDR in 1950. What stands here now went up between 2013 and 2020. Three of its facades are reconstructions of Schlueter. The fourth, facing the Spree, is openly modern.
buildings.tell: Walk right around it. On the Spree side the baroque stops and a flat modern facade takes over, with no attempt to pretend. That deliberate break is the building telling you the truth about itself.

buildings.name: Berlin Cathedral
buildings.today: Finished in 1905. The lantern on top of the dome caught fire in 1944 and fell through into the church. East Germany decided to rebuild in 1975 and finished in 1993, but in a simplified form: the dome and the four corner towers each came back sixteen metres lower than they were, and the Memorial Church wing was not rebuilt at all.
buildings.tell: Compare the cathedral with any pre-war photograph on a postcard rack nearby. The silhouette is flatter and the small towers have lost their lanterns. The walls you are standing next to are original; the crown above them is not the one Wilhelm II paid for.

buildings.name: Altes Museum
buildings.fabricLine: Schinkel stone outside, post-war work inside
buildings.today: Karl Friedrich Schinkel built it between 1825 and 1828 and it opened in 1830. An ammunition wagon parked against the building exploded on 8 May 1945 and burnt it out. The rebuild ran from 1951 to 1966 and was faithful outside, but the surviving fragments of the Cornelius frescoes in the colonnade were removed rather than saved.
buildings.tell: The eighteen sandstone columns facing the Lustgarten are Schinkel. Step inside to the rotunda and the stair hall and you are in a post-war interior, with a glass front that only dates from 1993.

buildings.name: Neues Museum
buildings.fabricLine: Original fabric plus visible new work, reopened 2009
buildings.today: Friedrich August Stueler built it between 1843 and 1855. It was bombed, then left open to the Berlin weather for more than fifty years. David Chipperfield restored it between 1999 and 2009 and refused to hide the damage, so shell holes, scorched brick and half-lost murals were stabilised and left visible next to plainly new surfaces.
buildings.tell: This is the one building in Berlin where you do not need a test, because it answers the question for you in every room. If you only visit one place after reading this, make it this one.

buildings.name: Alte Nationalgalerie
buildings.fabricLine: Original shell, rebuilt in stages from 1948
buildings.today: Planned by Stueler from 1862 and finished by Johann Heinrich Strack in 1876. Bombing and the street fighting of 1945 left it badly damaged. Clearance began in 1947, rebuilding in 1948, and part of the building reopened as early as June 1949. The last repairs were finished in 1966 and a full restoration ran to 2001.
buildings.tell: Look at the great outdoor staircase and the temple front. That shape is original. The building took its damage mostly inside and at roof level, which is exactly the part visitors never see.

buildings.name: Zeughaus
buildings.today: The oldest building on Unter den Linden, begun in 1695 and finished in 1706. It burnt out in the war and was rebuilt between 1948 and 1965. Practical note for your trip: the Zeughaus and the permanent German history exhibition have been closed for renovation since June 2021, and the German Historical Museum is running its exhibitions in the neighbouring Pei Building instead.
buildings.tell: Go into the courtyard, which is open when the museum forecourt is. The twenty-two carved heads of dying warriors by Andreas Schlueter around the walls are original baroque sculpture and among the best things in Berlin that nobody queues for.

buildings.name: Staatsoper Unter den Linden
buildings.today: Built for Frederick the Great between 1741 and 1743 to plans by Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff. It burnt to its foundation walls in the night of 18 to 19 August 1843 and was rebuilt to the old drawings inside a year. Then it burnt again in the war and was rebuilt between 1951 and 1955. A further renovation ran from 2010 to 2017.
buildings.tell: The pediment relief showing music among the arts is by Ernst Rietschel and dates from 1844, not 1743. It arrived with the first rebuild, which is a useful reminder that the war was not the only thing that reset Berlin buildings.
